paragraphs.heading: Making numbers no one can guess
paragraphs.text: Random number generation is the job of producing a string of numbers or symbols that nobody can forecast any better than pure chance would allow. The tool that does it is called a random number generator, or RNG. Looking back over the output, you may spot some patterns, but you could never have seen them coming in advance.

paragraphs.heading: Why people need randomness
paragraphs.text: Random numbers are put to work in gambling, statistical sampling, computer simulation, cryptography and completely randomized experimental designs, wherever an outcome should be unpredictable. Not every use asks for the same strength. Cryptography and some numerical methods need output that looks very random indeed, while a random quote of the day or the next move of a computer opponent in a game needs only a little unpredictability.

paragraphs.heading: Dice, coins and printed tables
paragraphs.text: Some ways of making random results are ancient: rolling dice, flipping coins, shuffling cards and casting yarrow stalks for the I Ching. Because these are mechanical, getting lots of good random numbers out of them, which statistics needs, took a great deal of time and effort. So the results were sometimes gathered and handed out as tables of random numbers. Dice, coins and roulette wheels are still used today, mostly for games and gambling, since they are too slow for most statistical or cryptographic work.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the physical world
paragraphs.text: The first main method measures something in nature that is expected to behave randomly, then corrects for any bias in the measuring. Sources include atmospheric noise, thermal noise, cosmic background radiation and radioactive decay. Generators built this way are called hardware random number generators, or HRNGs, and they usually give only a limited number of random bits each second. How fast they run depends on the physical process being measured, so they are called blocking: they must wait until enough unpredictability, called entropy, has been gathered to meet demand.

paragraphs.heading: Following a recipe from a seed
paragraphs.text: The second main method runs a computer algorithm that turns a short starting value, the seed, into a long sequence that only looks random. Such a pseudorandom number generator, or PRNG, is fully determined by its seed, so anyone who knows the seed can reproduce the whole sequence. It does not have to wait on outside events, so large batches of output can be read from it without waiting. Computational methods like this all fall short of true randomness, which generally rules them out for cryptography.

paragraphs.heading: When repeatability helps
paragraphs.text: That predictability can be an advantage. In Monte Carlo simulations, starting again from the same seed replays the exact same numbers, which makes hunting down bugs easier. A PRNG can even serve in cryptography as long as the seed stays secret, since a sender and a receiver can then produce the same numbers to use as keys. Specially designed cryptographically secure generators, called CSPRNGs, also exist for this kind of work.

paragraphs.heading: Mixing the two methods
paragraphs.text: In practice the two approaches are often combined. A hardware generator supplies the seed, and a faster PRNG stretches it into a larger stream of output. Standard cryptographic designs work this way, harvesting randomness from nature to seed a CSPRNG.
